The Lucas gusher at Spindletop; the first major gusher of the Texas Oil Boom which led to the creation of Gulf Oil and Texaco. 1901

Spindletop is a salt dome oil field located in the southern portion of Beaumont, Texas. On January 10, 1901, a well at Spindletop struck oil and blew for nine days at a rate estimated at 100,000 barrels (16,000 m3) of oil per day. Gulf Oil and Texaco, now part of Chevron Corporation, were formed to develop production at Spindletop.

The frenzy of oil exploration and the economic development it generated in the state became known as the Texas Oil Boom. The United States soon became the world's leading oil producer.

In 1899 Anthony Lucas became a drilling contractor and leased land south of Beaumont. In need of money, Lucas persuaded John H. Galey and James M. Guffey, associates of the Mellon family from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to join the project.

After reaching the depth of 370 metres (1,210 ft), at 10:30 AM on January 10, 1901, natural gas erupted followed by a stream of crude oil reaching 60 metres (200 ft). The eruption lasted nine days until stopped by one of Lucas's devices. The "Lucas Gusher" was the largest gusher ever seen and produced around 100,000 barrels (16,000 m3) of oil a day. The occasion was witnessed by about 50,000 spectators. The population of Beaumont mushroomed from 8,000 to 60,000 within a year. By 1902 as many as 285 wells were operating on Spindletop Hill and over 600 oil companies had been chartered. Lucas possessed just a tiny share in a company he helped to establish. Because of this and other reasons, he left the company at the end of 1901.

A few thoughts. I am going to try to make this understandable for a lay man (sorry if i fail at it)
Those extractors don't usually work for seized bolts.

To calculate the proper drilling speed the formula is as follows: "Cutting speed in surface feet per minute{SFM} * 12 / (drill diameter * pi). Cutting speed for mild steel is 100SFM. Since bolts are usually harder than mild steel i would recommend something like 50SFM or lower.

When you had the drill going the wrong way, even just one rotation, the bit is wrecked and needs resharpening. The cutting edges are very sharp and break easily going in reverse.

I also can see that the relief angle of the drill (the part behind the cutting edge) is negative. Meaning the area behind the cutting edge is higher than the cutting edge itself. The drill is cutting with it's ass, you can't cut anything with a ball either. All you are accomplishing with your high speed, that drill geometry and high feed (pressing down on the drill hard), is to melt material and then pick it up a bit with the drill.

Cutting oil is important. Good cutting oils have extreme pressure additives. The oil is there to lubricate the tool and prevent the metal that is being removed to stick to the tool, which looks like is what happened to you. Lubricants also aide in cooling the tool and the work piece. When tool and/or material get to hot they can start welding to each other. Another thing happened to you.

When adding cutting oil, or any coolant, make sure to have a steady stream of it on the work area. Don't let the part get hot and then cool it off, as this can potentially work harden the material. This would make drilling even more difficult and in some cases impossible with regular drill bits.
You might have work hardened the material already. getting through that is tricky. Try with a new bit, a good cutting oil, low speed and high feed. (I would round off the cutting edge a bit to make it stronger, but that is something probably better left to a machinist.)

Most grades of steel can work harden, and drilling at high speed, high pressure will do it with a large surface area bit. Additionally, friction generates heat with can remove the temper on your drill bits, leaving you with a work hard bolt, and a soft bit (which will dull instantly, and actually increase your problems)

Slow down your drill speed, use a 1/8 or 3/32 bit to start with along with some coolant. WD-40 will work in a pinch. Peck into the bolt a bit, spray some lube. Peck some more, spray. take a break if things start to get hot. Rinse and repeat as necessary, then move up to a larger drill size. Remember drill bits are cutting tools, so you should be seeing chips and curls coming from the work piece. If all you see is dust, your grinding, not cutting.

You are NOT supposed to go in revers with the drill bit. And you are not supposed to drill out the entire bolt with an extractor set. You drill, in the clockwise direction like all other drill bits, just enough to make a hole into which the extractor goes into. The extractor has a reverse thread. The extractor is NOT A DRILL BIT. The extractor is turned in the opposite direction, SLOWLY, applying a lot of pressure so that it catches the bolt and causes it to spin.

You have dulled out your drill bits. You were using it wrong.
